doc.title: Sheila Jordan — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Moving between styles: melody before lyrics
summary: Asked about working from bebop to George Russell and Roswell Rudd, she says she does not think in styles and chooses songs for their melody rather than lyrics.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Well, let‟s talk about your stylistic breadth. I mean, you know, singing bebop, but then George kinda takes you into the stratosphere funk.
And then you‟re working with Roswell Rudd. So you seem to be comfortable… I mean, for the sake of discussion, we as jazz musicians don‟t really want to put labels and…
But Roswell Rudd is not an inside player, known as an inside player. Nor is George really…

So you seem to be able to go in and out, if we can use those, that as the vernacular. So working with Roswell or… and we can come back and talk about that specifically, but how do you feel about stylistically being able to go in and out?

I don‟t even think of style. I just think of how I feel and if I like the music and if I like, if I like the lyrics or if, if I just, if I‟m moved by… See, I‟m different from most singers. They listen for the lyrics first, that‟s what they listen to first. I‟m the total opposite. I listen to the melody first. „Cause if it‟s not a good melody and it doesn‟t move me and I don‟t feel it can go anywhere, I don‟t, I don‟t want to do the tune. You could have tremendous lyrics, but with lyrics, you can change them. Well, if you have to be careful if you record them, though, nowadays.
